newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian Franki looking for global partner.
newsitem.headline: Belgian Franki looking for global partner.

text.p: Belgian construction group Franki NV said on Tuesday it was looking for one or more partners to help manage its global foundations businesses and return the group to profitability after three poor years.
"We think we can conclude an alliance before the end of (1997)," Franki chairman and chief executive officer Johan De Muynck said at a news conference on 1996 earnings.
"At this stage we have several options. What we know for sure is that we want to increase our profitability and the success of the Franki organisation," he added.
Franki said group net losses narrowed to 137 million Belgian francs in 1996 from a loss of 255 million francs in 1995 and a loss of 458 million francs in 1994.
The group last made a profit of 76 million francs in 1993, when it paid its last dividend of 13 francs gross.
Franki said it would again skip its dividend in 1996 and reiterated that payments would not resume until the group was back in the black.
De Muynck said it was too soon to forecast whether the group would return to profit in 1997.

"I am not very optimistic for the short term," he said. "Thankfully, in certain areas of the world profitability is not in danger and we hope to return to profit in Latin America. However, I remain prudent for North America and extremely prudent for Europe, where it's dangerous to be too optimistic."
Investments would total 200 million francs in 1997, down from 278 million in 1996 and 263 million in 1995.

"We have made strong investments in the Asia/Pacific region in the last two years. We think this is sufficient for now. Should there be a change in the market we would revise that strategy," De Muynck said.

De Muynck also declined to predict how Franki's foundations activities -- which account for the bulk of group sales -- could be affected by an alliance. The impact would depend on what form a partnership took, he said. No negotiations had started and the group would take its time about finding a partner, he said.

He said the search for a partner, which he hinted last year might take place, was prompted by the high capital costs of the foundations business and the fact Franki's activities outside Europe were spread too thinly around the world.

Foundation activities, such as the anchoring of roof supports at Sydney's Olympic stadium, accounted for 6.09 billion francs, or 55 percent of 1996 sales (including Latin American operations, which are not consolidated at group level).
In Europe, civil engineering and other building activities had sales of 4.56 billion francs against Franki's European foundation activites sales of 3.12 billion francs.

Sales in Asia (1.30 billion francs), Africa (938 million), Latin America (635 million) and North America (451 million) remained dominated by foundations activities, finance manager Frans de Ridder said.

De Ridder said Franki's Foraky deep drilling unit, which secured a two billion franc, two-year contract in El Salvador last November, was not intended to be included in any alliance, although it is presently held through the European foundations business unit.
